newsitem.title: CANADA: IPL, Suncor combine pipeline plans.
newsitem.headline: IPL, Suncor combine pipeline plans.

text.p: IPL Energy Inc and Suncor Energy Inc said on Monday they would combine their Alberta pipeline proposals into one C$325 million project, the latest twist in a race to boost transport capacity for fast-growing Canadian heavy oil production.

The companies said the new project would have capacity of more than 500,000 barrels a day, enough to meet the requirements of Suncor's expanding oil sands plant near Fort McMurray, Alberta and the needs of other shippers identified by IPL. Under the agreement, IPL would build the pipeline and Suncor would operate it, the Calgary-based firms said.

The move came two weeks after Alberta Energy Co Ltd and Husky Oil Ltd announced plans for their joint Lakeland Pipeline system, a C$400 million project with an initial capacity of 150,000 barrels of heavy oil a day.
Shell Canada Ltd has also served notice it might build a pipeline to its Scotford refinery in Edmonton from its proposed oil sands project in Alberta's Athabasca region.
IPL said its 30-inch line would extend to Hardisty, Alberta from Fort McMurray via the Cold Lake heavy oil region in northeastern Alberta, similar to the AEC/Husky proposal.

Hardisty, southeast of Edmonton, is a key connection point for IPL's Interprovincial Pipe Line system to U.S. Midwest and eastern Canadian refining markets. It is also the starting point of the new Express Pipeline to Wyoming.
The companies said Suncor, which originally proposed its own line to ship production from its expanding oil sands operation, would commit volumes under a long-term agreement.
Interprovincial President Pat Daniel said in early May his firm's executives were in talks with northern Alberta heavy oil and oil sands producers with the aim of combining all the projects into one.

At the time, Daniel singled out Suncor as a key player in the talks because its plans were more advanced than the others. Suncor said last year it was planning a C$250 million, 55,000 barrel a day line.

"When we made that announcement in December, we were approached by a variety of pipeline operators who said, 'Hey, we're the experts in this business and you're not.' We agreed with them," Suncor spokeswoman Patti Lewis said in a telephone interview from Fort McMurray.
"The bottom line for us is to get our product to market and if they can do it in a cost-effective way, we'll let them."
AEC Pipelines manager of business development Paul Reimer said the competing proposal would not cool AEC's and Husky's resolve to build their own three-phase system.

"The Suncor and Interprovincial marriage is disappointing from the standpoint that we were hopeful that Suncor would join Lakeland Pipeline," Reimer said. "But that doesn't mean for a moment that Lakeland Pipelines' plans change at all."
He said the Fort McMurray region was a big base for several other operators that it planned to woo to its line.
Pending regulatory approval, construction on the IPL/Suncor pipeline would start late this year for completion in late 1998.
Construction of the 24-inch Lakeland Pipeline was slated to start in September. It, too, requires a green light from regulators.
